content: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is a neurological disorder characterized by progressive or relapsing and remitting paralysis. It is believed to result from an autoimmune response, and corticosteroid treatment is thought to be beneficial for managing this condition. Prednisone and prednisolone are two commonly used corticosteroids, typically administered as oral tablets. Prednisone is metabolized in the liver into prednisolone, so their effects are generally equivalent. Dexamethasone, another corticosteroid, is more potent and is used in smaller doses. A systematic review of corticosteroid treatment for CIDP was first published in 2001 and last updated in 2015. This update aimed to identify any new evidence regarding the efficacy of corticosteroids in treating CIDP. The primary objective was to evaluate the effects of corticosteroid treatment compared to placebo or no treatment, as well as to compare different corticosteroid regimens. A search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted on November 8, 2016, using databases such as the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and Embase. Clinical trial registries were also reviewed for ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria required RCTs or quasi-RCTs involving corticosteroid or adrenocorticotrophic hormone treatment for CIDP, diagnosed according to internationally accepted definitions. Two authors independently extracted data from the included studies and assessed the risk of bias. The primary outcome of interest was the change in disability, while secondary outcomes included changes in impairment after 12 weeks and the occurrence of side effects. The strength of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. One non-blinded RCT compared oral prednisone with no treatment in 35 participants. However, this study did not measure the primary outcome of the systematic review. The trial had a high risk of bias. After 12 weeks, 12 out of 19 participants treated with prednisone showed improvement in Neuropathy Impairment Scale scores, compared to 5 out of 16 participants in the no-treatment group. The risk ratio (RR) for improvement was 2.02 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.90 to 4.52), but the evidence quality was very low. Side effects were not reported in detail, although one participant in the prednisone group died. Another double-blind RCT compared daily standard-dose oral prednisolone with monthly high-dose oral dexamethasone in 40 participants. This study did not report any of the prespecified outcomes for the review. The trial had a low risk of bias, but the evidence quality was limited due to the small sample size. There was little or no difference in the number of participants achieving remission (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.50 to 2.45, favoring monthly dexamethasone) or in changes in disability or impairment after one year. Grip strength and Medical Research Council (MRC) scores also showed little or no difference between the two groups. Eight out of 16 participants in the prednisolone group and seven out of 24 participants in the dexamethasone group experienced deterioration. Side effects were similar between the two regimens, but sleeplessness was less common with monthly dexamethasone (low-quality evidence), and moon facies (a rounded, moon-shaped facial appearance) was also less frequent with dexamethasone (moderate-quality evidence). Observational studies and clinical experience suggest that corticosteroids are beneficial for CIDP, but long-term use is associated with serious side effects. The evidence from the only RCT comparing oral prednisone with no treatment is of very low quality, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions. High-dose monthly oral dexamethasone appears to have similar efficacy to daily standard-dose oral prednisolone, with some differences in side effect profiles. Specifically, moon facies and sleeplessness may be less common with dexamethasone. Further research is needed to identify factors that predict treatment response and to better understand the long-term effects of corticosteroid therapy in CIDP.
